summary: Defines rules for encoding data modeled with YANG in the Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR). YANG describes configuration data, state data, and the inputs and outputs of operations, and this document gives a compact binary form for them, suited to small devices. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: YANG describes what information a device has, and CBOR is a short way to write it down. This is the guide for turning one into the other so messages come out small.

questions: how to encode yang data in cbor
how are yang types encoded in cbor
subtitle: How YANG-modeled configuration and state data is written as compact CBOR for small devices and slow networks.

tldr.problem: YANG data already had XML and JSON encodings, which are bulky for constrained nodes and constrained networks.
tldr.mechanism: YANG-CBOR serializes each container, list entry or similar node as a CBOR map, keyed either by compact numeric YANG Schema Item iDentifiers (SIDs, sent as deltas) or by text names, and maps each YANG type to a specific CBOR type.
tldr.outcome: It defines the application/yang-data+cbor media type with id=sid and id=name variants and registers CBOR tags 43 to 47.

today: RFC 9254 is a Proposed Standard; no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why a CBOR Encoding for YANG
sections.content:
YANG 1.1 (RFC 7950) defines an XML encoding for data instances such as configuration datastores, state data, RPC and action inputs and outputs, and notifications. RFC 7951 added a JSON encoding. RFC 9254 adds a third set of rules, collectively called YANG-CBOR, based on the Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR, RFC 8949).

The result is more compact than XML and JSON and more suitable for constrained nodes and constrained networks, as defined by RFC 7228. The reader is assumed to know both YANG and CBOR.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing a device's settings in long words wastes space on tiny gadgets. CBOR is like shorthand, so the same information fits in a much smaller note.

sections.title: SIDs and Names as Keys
sections.content:
A representation node such as a container, list entry, notification, RPC input or output, or anydata node is serialized as a CBOR map. Each schema node inside it becomes a key and a value. Two kinds of key are supported, and a protocol may mandate one or let the generator choose per key.

A YANG Schema Item iDentifier (SID) is an unsigned integer limited to 63 bits. SIDs identify identities, data nodes, RPCs, actions, YANG data structures, notifications, modules and features. When used as map keys they are sent as deltas: signed integers added to the reference SID of the map. The outermost map has reference SID zero unless the environment says otherwise, and for most inner maps the reference is the SID of the entry they are embedded in. Where an absolute SID is wanted in a key position, it is tagged with CBOR tag number 47. SID value 0 is reserved and never used in interchange. How SIDs are assigned is outside this document.

A name is a text string in the style of the JSON encoding: either simple (foo) or namespace-qualified with the module name (example-foomod:top). A namespace-qualified name MUST be used for all members of a top-level map, and whenever a node's namespace differs from its parent's; otherwise the simple form MUST be used. Names avoid SID management but make the data significantly larger.
sections.plainLanguage: Every item can be called by a long name or by a short number. Numbers are shorter, and a number can even be written as how far it is from the one before it.

sections.title: Encoding Nodes of the Data Tree
sections.content:
The node kinds map to CBOR as follows.

  • A leaf is encoded by its datatype, using the rules of the type section.
  • A container, YANG data structure, notification content, RPC or action input or output, and each list entry are CBOR maps (major type 5). The RFC calls these container-like instances.
  • A leaf-list is a CBOR array (major type 4) of entries encoded by their datatype.
  • A list is an array of maps, one per entry. This applies even to a list with a single entry.
  • anydata is encoded like a container; anyxml can hold any CBOR data item (the "xml" is a misnomer inherited from YANG-XML).

When SIDs are keys, the delta is the node's SID minus the SID of its parent container, list, RPC, action or notification. For example, a hostname leaf can be written as {1752 : "myhost.example.com"}, or with a name as {"ietf-system:hostname" : "myhost.example.com"}. SID numbers in the examples are illustrative and do not allocate anything.

The document says decoders SHALL support indefinite-length encoding unless the protocol says otherwise, and that nodes that are instantiated but empty are encoded with length zero. A payload SHOULD include enough information for each node to be identified statelessly, for example a SID, a delta, a qualified name or an instance-identifier.

The yang-data extension (RFC 8040) is encoded as a container: a map with a single pair, keyed by the SID or the namespace-qualified name of the extension's container.
sections.plainLanguage: Boxes become labeled folders, lists become stacks of folders, and each setting is written inside using the shortest label that still tells you what it is.

sections.title: How YANG Types Become CBOR
sections.content:
Each YANG built-in type has a required CBOR form.

  • uint8 to uint64: unsigned integer. int8 to int64: unsigned or negative integer by value.
  • decimal64: a CBOR decimal fraction; 2.57 with two fraction digits is 4([-2, 257]).
  • string: text string. boolean: true or false. binary: byte string. empty: null.
  • enumeration: the integer value of the enum. leafref: the encoding of the node it references.
  • bits: a byte string, or an array alternating byte strings and positive integers that move the bit offset in units of 8 bits. Trailing zero bytes are never generated, and a single-element array MUST instead be just the byte string.
  • identityref: a SID (unsigned integer, no delta) or a text name; a name from a different module than the leaf must be namespace-qualified.
  • instance-identifier: for a single-instance node, the SID; for a list entry, an array of the SID followed by the key values in key order; or, with names, an XPath-like text string.

Inside a union, four types are wrapped in CBOR tags so they cannot be confused with other types encoded the same way: bits, enumeration, identityref and instance-identifier. Within a union, enumeration and bits are encoded as text strings, for example 44("unbounded"). The RFC explains this adds complexity but keeps compatibility with how overlapping unions work in XML and JSON.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of value has its own way to be written down: numbers as numbers, words as words, yes-or-no as yes-or-no. Tricky ones get a little sticker saying what they are.

sections.title: Content-Types
sections.content:
The document defines the media type application/yang-data+cbor, usable without parameters or with an id parameter set to name or sid. The body is a CBOR map from names and/or SIDs to instance values.

  • id=sid: for applications that need to be frugal with space and text processing, such as those on constrained nodes.
  • id=name: for applications that do not want SID management and have ample resources; it is a direct, more efficient substitute for the JSON media type.
  • no id: for more complex applications that benefit from SIDs but must also handle YANG modules that have no SID mapping yet. Both forms may appear.

How a transfer protocol selects among them is out of scope. The RFC points to the last paragraph of Section 5.2 of RFC 8040 for RESTCONF and to the Content-Format and Accept Options of CoAP (RFC 7252).
sections.plainLanguage: There are three labels that tell a receiver whether the message uses short numbers, long names, or a mix.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8949 and RFC 7950 apply. The encoding adds no new issues beyond those of the protocol that carries it. Receivers SHOULD reject messages that do not follow these rules and reply with an error. When the id parameter is used, identifiers of the other type should be rejected so that implementations do not read the same content differently.

With SIDs, correct interpretation also depends on having the right SID mapping information, so managing that mapping needs the same care as managing the YANG modules.
sections.plainLanguage: If a message does not follow the rules, throw it back. And make sure everyone uses the same number-to-name dictionary, or they will misread each other.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the media type application/yang-data+cbor with an optional id parameter. It also added three CoAP Content-Formats: ID 340 for the plain type, 341 for id=name and 140 for id=sid.

Five CBOR tags were allocated: 43 (bits), 44 (enumeration), 45 (identityref), 46 (instance-identifier) and 47 (YANG SID).
sections.plainLanguage: The official lists of names and numbers got new entries so everyone uses the same label for this format.

items.label: bits
items.desc: Text string; YANG bits type inside a union.

items.label: enumeration
items.desc: Text string; YANG enumeration type inside a union.

items.label: instance-identifier
items.desc: Unsigned integer, text string or array.

items.label: YANG SID
items.desc: Unsigned integer; marks an absolute SID instead of a delta.
